name: Hana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I work at Berg's, the family supermarket on Church Street in our town, and I've been there since I left school, so nine years. I open the tills at seven, do the morning rush, and after lunch I'm on the deli counter slicing ham and cheese for the same forty or fifty people every week. Mr Berg still comes in every day at seventy-one, and his son runs the ordering now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's ours, in a way. People ask for me by name at the deli, and when Mrs Olsen's husband died I took her shopping round to her house myself for a month. What wears me out is the new discount store at the edge of town, because every week someone tells me it's cheaper there and I have to smile. I'm engaged to Jonas, he's just finished his carpentry apprenticeship, and we're getting married next June at St Peter's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never trusted it anyway, and I'd be glad. At Berg's we'd laugh about it, because Mr Berg still writes the specials on a chalkboard. I don't go online much, but at church I'd say it's good that people are still needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, AI was never my worry, the discount store is. Since it opened last year our Saturday takings are down, and Mr Berg's son already cut Sunday afternoons. If nothing changes with AI, I'm still in a small shop fighting a big one, and that's what I lie awake about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working my hours and do whatever extra they need, like stocking on Saturdays. Jonas and I would keep putting money aside for the wedding and for a deposit, about three hundred a month between us. I'd keep away from all the AI things, I don't need them to slice ham.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but not easy. Berg's is still the worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sunday afternoons were cut. What did that cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five hours a week, which is roughly the flowers budget for the wedding, if I'm honest. Jonas said we could make the arches ourselves, he's a carpenter after all. But it hurt, because it was the quiet shift I liked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if Berg's closes, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the discount store or the big supermarket in the next town, I suppose, which is a forty-minute bus. They'd probably take me, I've got nine years on tills. But it wouldn't be the same, nobody there knows Mrs Olsen takes her ham thin.

say: I **never trusted** it anyway, and I'd be glad to be right.
It's good that **people are still needed**, and I'd say so at church.
think: AI was never the worry; the **discount store** is, with Saturday takings already down.
Sunday afternoons were **cut by five hours**, and more cuts could follow.
do: Keep working her hours and take **extra Saturday** stocking shifts.
Keep saving about **three hundred a month** with Jonas for the wedding and a deposit.
feel: **Relieved** about AI, but still uneasy about Berg's future.
S0.quote: AI was never my worry, the discount store is.
fieldNote: Her main pressure is **local competition**, which AI Plateau leaves untouched.
Strong sense of **belonging**: the shop, the customers, the church.
Already lost five hours a week; the **wedding budget** is how she measures money.

steps.text: Keep the deli and till shifts and offer Saturday stocking
Save three hundred a month with Jonas for wedding and deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the computers that should worry, not the shopkeepers. At Berg's I'd tell the customers we'll always have a person at the till while I'm there. My mother would agree with me, she says the same about the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid Mr Berg's son would put in self-checkouts. He's been to the trade fair twice and he talks about the discount store's costs all the time. If he does, I'm not the one who'll be keen to stand next to the machines and help, and he knows that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the son straight out what his plans are, because I'd rather know. I'd ask for more deli hours, since slicing to order isn't something a computer does. Jonas and I would cut back, maybe a smaller wedding, and I'd ask my parents if we could stay with them for a year to save for the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I think. It's the feeling of the shop changing under me without anyone asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't be keen to help with the machines. Would you learn if it saved your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do it if I had to, I'm not stupid. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it, and he'd see that. There's a girl, Freja, who's nineteen and loves all that, and she'd get the hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Mr Berg's son, really, he's trying to keep the doors open. I'd blame the big chains and people who drive out of town to save twenty pence on milk. If people shopped locally, none of this would be needed.

say: It's the **computers** that should worry, not the shopkeepers.
There'll always be a **person at the till** at Berg's while I'm there.
think: Mr Berg's son may install **self-checkouts** to match the discount store's costs.
A younger colleague who loves machines would likely **get the hours** instead of her.
do: Ask Mr Berg's son **straight out** about his plans.
Ask for more **deli hours**, where slicing to order needs a person.
Plan a **smaller wedding** and live with her parents for a year.
feel: **Anxious**, as if the shop is changing under her without anyone asking.
S1.quote: I'd blame the big chains and people who drive out of town to save twenty pence on milk.
fieldNote: Admits her **resistance** to technology could cost her hours to a younger colleague.
Blames **out-of-town chains** and shoppers, not the owner's family.
Leans on **family**, not the state: moving in with her parents to save.

steps.text: Ask for more hours on the deli counter
Cut the wedding guest list and budget
Move in with her parents for a year to save a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and someone should slow it down. At church we'd pray about it, and I'd mean it. I'd say people need to look after their own, because the government won't be quick enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the paperwork side of Berg's, the ordering and the pricing, goes straight away in 2028, and that's the son's job, so he'll be watching every penny. Then by 2031 robots can do the tills and the stocking. Berg's would either buy the machines or close, and either way I'm out within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jonas we keep the wedding but make it small, the church and a lunch at my parents', and put the rest straight into savings. I'd ask my aunt about working in her bakery, because she's always said I'm good with dough. And I'd vote for whoever promises to protect small local shops, even if I don't usually think much of politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, the way you are when you hear the shop's being sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jonas is a carpenter. Does that make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because his work is all hands. But if robots can do hands-on work by 2031, then a robot can hang a door, can't it? So we'd have about three years where he's safer than me, and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't usually like handouts. Would you take government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'd worked and paid in, yes, I would, and I wouldn't feel ashamed. I'd rather a job, though. My grandfather said you take help to get back up, not to stay down.

say: It's **frightening**, and someone should slow it down.
People need to **look after their own**, because government won't be quick enough.
think: The **ordering and pricing** go in 2028; robots could take the tills by 2031.
Berg's would **buy machines or close**, and either way she's out within five years.
do: Keep the wedding but make it **small**, with savings going straight to the cushion.
Ask her aunt about work in the **family bakery**.
Vote for whoever promises to **protect local shops**.
feel: **Scared**, like hearing the shop is being sold.
S2.quote: My grandfather said you take help to get back up, not to stay down.
fieldNote: Sees clearly how **thinking AI** squeezes the owner first, then robots reach her.
Fears both incomes go, since **carpentry** is hands-on too.
Traditional views bend: she'd accept **government help** if she'd paid in.
Unusually willing to engage in **politics** to protect small shops.

steps.text: Hold a small church wedding with lunch at her parents' house
Ask her aunt for regular shifts in the family bakery
Vote for candidates who promise to protect small local shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives families time to plan, and that's what they should do. At work I'd tell Mr Berg we should be the friendly shop, the one with people, for as long as we can. I'd say it to the customers too, to keep them coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years and three more for the robots is eight years at Berg's, if Berg's lasts. I'd be thirty-five, probably with a baby, and I don't want to be retraining then. So the time matters, but it doesn't change where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have the wedding as planned next June, then save hard for a house with Jonas, about four hundred a month. I'd start working Saturdays at my aunt's bakery to learn bread properly, because people will still pay for bread made by someone they know. I'd stay at Berg's in the week as long as there's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could breathe. It's not like the two-year one, where it felt like the floor going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people will pay for bread made by someone they know. Even if a robot bakes it cheaper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some will, the ones who care. Mrs Olsen would. Maybe not enough people to pay a wage, I don't know that, and I won't pretend I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the nineteen-year-old, Freja, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to learn the machines, because she likes them and she'll be young enough to move with them. That's not for me. Everyone has their own thing to be good at.

say: **Five years** gives families time to plan.
Berg's should be **the friendly shop**, the one with people, for as long as it can.
think: She gets about **eight years** at Berg's, if Berg's lasts.
The extra time **doesn't change the end**, just when she faces it with a baby.
do: Keep the **June wedding** and save four hundred a month for a house.
Work Saturdays at her aunt's **bakery** to learn bread properly.
Stay at Berg's **in the week** while there's work.
feel: **Worried**, but able to breathe, unlike the two-year picture.
S3.quote: People will still pay for bread made by someone they know.
fieldNote: Extra time lets her keep **family plans** intact.
Bets on **trust and craft** over price, while admitting she can't prove it.
Still expects to **lose the till job**, so her income risk stays real.

steps.text: Hold the June wedding at St Peter's as planned
Work Saturdays at her aunt's bakery learning bread
Save four hundred a month with Jonas for a house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off, and we've heard all this before. At church I'd say what I always say, trust in hard work and each other. I wouldn't change much in what I tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, by 2039 I'd be forty, hopefully with two children, and I think I'd be working part-time anyway. Jonas would have his own workshop by then, he hopes. So it touches us, but it lands when I'm more at home, and that's what I want anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Berg's and keep the Saturdays at my aunt's bakery for something to fall back on. We'd have the wedding and try for children in a year or two. I'd wait and see what the robots actually do before changing anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like a cloud on the horizon. Nothing I'd change my life for today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be working part-time anyway. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Jonas's workshop does well, yes, just. If it doesn't, no, and then I'd need a job, and that's when the robots arrive. So I suppose it's not as safe as I said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew for certain it was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing in the first years, if I'm honest. I don't like changing things on a guess. I'd watch what happens at the big supermarkets first, they'll get the machines before Berg's.

say: **Ten years** is a long way off, and we've heard all this before.
Trust in **hard work** and each other, as I always say at church.
think: By **2039** she expects to be forty, with children, and working part-time.
Her plan rests on Jonas's **workshop** doing well, which she admits isn't certain.
do: Carry on at Berg's and keep **Saturday bakery** shifts as a fallback.
Go ahead with the wedding and try for **children** in a year or two.
**Watch the big supermarkets** before changing anything major.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a cloud on the horizon, nothing to change her life for.
S4.quote: I don't like changing things on a guess.
fieldNote: Long warning fits her **resistant** nature; she waits for proof.
Catches her own **contradiction** about part-time work and accepts it.
Household safety depends on Jonas's **workshop**, a hands-on trade that robots reach late.

steps.text: Keep working weekdays at Berg's tills and deli
Try for children within a year or two of the wedding
Watch how big supermarkets use robots before changing plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, the two-year one, because Berg's would go and Jonas might follow three years later, and we'd only just be married. What would help is shoppers choosing local shops, and maybe a rule that small shops get some help to stay open with people in them. And family, honestly, my parents and my aunt are my plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. It sounds old-fashioned, but at St Peter's, our church, we look after each other when someone loses work. I don't think anyone's building a machine for that.

headlineQuote: At St Peter's, our church, we look after each other when someone loses work.
portrait: Hana, 27, has worked the **tills and deli** at Berg's, a family supermarket in her small town, for nine years.
She is engaged to Jonas, a newly qualified **carpenter**, and their wedding at St Peter's is next June.
Her biggest worry before AI is the **discount store** that already cost her five hours a week.
She avoids technology and leans on **family and church**, not retraining schemes.
Only the two-year AGI picture **alarms** her; with more time she keeps her wedding and family plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Berg's would close and Jonas's carpentry might follow three years later.
whatWouldHelp: Shoppers **choosing local** and help for small shops that keep people working.
Her **parents and aunt**, who she calls her real plan.
